The story presents diverse socioeconomic perspectives, primarily contrasting the working-class experience of Marnie (a longtime grocery store cashier) with the wealthy, controlling environment of the Pruitt family. Miss Emily, who could easily be written as a one-dimensional, elitist villain, is instead depicted as a complex, morally ambiguous character. Her difficult and often condescending behaviors—such as correcting Marnie's grammar, referring to cashiers as "those girls," and evaluating Marnie based on her looking "tired"—are presented convincingly as the result of her own background as a self-made businesswoman who clawed her way out of debt and values practical usefulness and sharp observation above all else.
